pageData.heading: How to protect yourself from scams
pageData.para: Learn about the latest scams, how to spot them and how to keep yourself safe.

commonScams.heading: Common types of scams
commonScams.subHeading: Scams are deliberately designed to deceive you. Remember, if it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.

cards.heading: SMS & email scams
cards.para: Messages might include a link to direct you to a fraudulent website or ask you for personal information

cards.heading: Online shopping scams​​
cards.para: What might look like a genuine website selling goods at low prices could actually be a scam.

cards.heading: Remote access scams​
cards.para: Where a scammer calls you and attempts to obtain access to your accounts or device, pretending to be from a well-known company.

cards.heading: Investment scams
cards.para: When a money making opportunity seem too good to be true.​​

cards.heading: Romance & dating scams
cards.para: Where someone you meet online may not be who they claim to be, and set out to steal your heart in order to defraud you.​

cards.heading: Scams that target businesses​
cards.para: Learn about the main types of scams your staff need to be able to recognise to protect your business.

cards.heading: Threat & penalty scams​
cards.para: Where a scammer uses threats of penalty or harm to extort money from their victims.

cards.heading: Job scams​
cards.para: Where a job opportunity appears to require little effort for a high financial reward and promises to make you money quickly.

cards.heading: Digital wallet scams​
cards.para: When you are contacted, usually by SMS or email, and trick you into sharing your card details. Scammers will use this information to enter your card details into a digital wallet on another phone, so they can spend your money.

steps.title: Stop
steps.desc: Does a call, email or text seem off? The best thing to do is stop. Take a breath.Real organizations won’t put you under pressure to act instantly.

steps.title: Check
steps.desc: Ask someone you trust or contact the organization the message claims to be from.

steps.title: Reject
steps.desc: If you’re unsure, hang up on the caller, delete the email, block the phone number.Change your passwords.

cards.heading: Fraudulent SMS & Emails
cards.subHeading: Be cautious of fraudulent messages claiming to be from banks. A legitimate bank will never send an SMS or email that:
cards.para:
• 🚫 Asks for your bank account details
  • 🚫 Requests your customer ID or password
  • 🚫 Asks you to share an OTP
  • 🚫 Contains a direct login link

For secure banking, always visit the bank’s official website by typing the URL in your browser or using the bank’s verified mobile app

cards.heading: How to Spot a Scam
cards.subHeading: Scammers mimic banks with urgent requests, fake links, and unusual emails to steal information.
cards.para:
• ⚠️ Messages or emails with spelling errors or poor grammar
  • ⚠️ Unusual email addresses or URLs that look similar but aren’t quite right
  • ⚠️ Urgent requests, such as "unlock your account" or "verify your identity"
  • ⚠️ Unexpected claims of winning prizes or cash rewards

cards.heading: What to Do
cards.para:
• ✅ Do not click on any links in suspicious messages
  • ✅ Avoid opening unexpected attachments, especially from unknown senders
  • ✅ Inspect links carefully—hover over them on a computer or press and hold on mobile to check the actual URL
  • ✅ Report the scam to the respective bank’s fraud department
  • ✅ Delete the suspicious message immediately
